profile.summary: The Psalms are a collection of prayers, regrets, supplications, thanksgivings and praises inspired by God and composed over many centuries. The book brings together the voice of human authors before the Lord, but at the same time it functions as an instruction for the people of God: it teaches how to live, how to suffer, how to worship and how to wait. His opening with Psalms 1 and 2 presents the two great axes of the book: the righteous who meditates in the law of the Lord and the Messianic king in contrast to the rebels of the nations. As the collection progresses, the reader finds the tension between the faithfulness of God and the failure of Israel, including the David dynasty, a tension that points beyond Israel's history to the hope fulfilled in Jesus Christ. The New Testament reads the Psalms as a decisive book to understand Christ: their humiliation, suffering, vindication, and reign. Still, the collection also maintains future expectations, such as the full realization of God's purposes for his people and the submission of the nations to the Messiah.
profile.setting: The work was born in the historical and liturgical context of ancient Israel, over approximately a thousand years, amidst the life of worship, pilgrimage, national crisis, exile and post-exile restoration. The psalms circulated in community and devotional uses, linked to the temple and the historical memory of Israel. Literally, the book is a carefully organized anthology in five parts, formed by smaller collections and gradually edited until it reaches its final form after Babylonian exile. The authorship is varied: many psalms are linked to David, but less than half receives this explicit association, and in several cases the indication of the title may mean authorship, dedication, thematic relationship or liturgical use. Therefore, there is caution regarding direct assignments and exact dates.

structure.label: Book 1
structure.description: Opening of the collection with the righteous who lives by the instruction of God and the predominance of the laments connected to David, culminating in final doxology.

structure.label: Book 2
structure.description: New phase of the collection, with psalms from different groups and authors; emphasizes the Messianic hope, the crisis of the David dynasty and ends with the note on David's prayers.

structure.label: Book 3
structure.description: Retake questions about the justice and power of God in the face of the prosperity of the wicked, the crisis of exile and the apparent collapse of the promise made to David.

structure.label: Book 4
structure.description: It responds to the crisis of exile by highlighting the Lord as a true king, the need for wisdom and piety, and the revision of the history of redemption to exile.

structure.label: Book 5
structure.description: He develops the movement of affliction, crying, deliverance and praise; he gathers collections such as the songs of pilgrimage, the great praise and the final psalms of worship, ending with hope and exaltation.

themes: sovereign action of God in the face of suffering and rebellion
Instruction for godly, wise and obedient life
Crisis and hope of the David dynasty, culminating in the Messiah
I love sorry, repentance, deliverance and restoration
Praise as the final answer of God's people and anticipation of the submission of the nations
readingKeys: Observe the frequent movement of the text between pain, request and renewed trust; many psalms do not hide anguish, but lead it to God.
Read the book as an organized collection: Psalms 1 and 2 function as a gateway, and each of the five books advances reflection on the righteous, the king, and the people of God.
Note how the themes of the Old Testament widen in the New Testament, especially in the Messianic reading of Jesus as the perfect righteous and the promised King.
profile.cautions: The authorship of many psalms is discussed: the titles may indicate author, recipient, dedication or subject, not necessarily who composed the poem. The dates are also not uniform, as the collection was formed over a long time and edited in stages, with final form completed after exile. The titles of the psalms and certain musical or liturgical terms are not always clear. In addition, there are differences in numbering between textual traditions and translations, which requires attention when consulting references.

dossier.narratedEra: The Psalms narrate and pray the life of Israel over many centuries, but the final framework of the book looks at the history of Israel from creation to Exile and then to the expected restoration. The notes also describe the use of the Psalterius at the time of Jesus, when he was already well known and was part of the Hebrew canon Writings.
dossier.compositionEra: The composition began in different periods, with poems emerging over about a thousand years and being recited and collected little by little. The edition of the Psalter in a single book was completed after Babylonian exile. The annexed introductions also note that many psalms linked to David may be of David, but the Hebrew le- in the title may mean "de", "dedicated," "respect of" or "per," so that traditional authorship and effective authorship should not be confused in all cases.

politics.title: Rebellion of nations against the government of the Lord
politics.detail: Psalm 2 is presented in response to the revolt of the nations and the wicked against the rule of God. The notes read it as an introduction to the theme of divine reign over a rebellious and sinful world, culminating in the Messiah's rule.
politics.readingImpact: This shifts the reading of Psalm 2 from mere royal poetry to a programmatic opening of the book: the political conflict is, above all, resistance to the lordship of God and his Anointed.

politics.title: The dynasty of David and its historic failure
politics.detail: The notes insist that the royal ideal of Psalms 1-2 and 72 was not reached either by the people of Israel or by the kings of the dynasty of David. The whole book records this failure and therefore points to another hope.
politics.readingImpact: The reader is led to see the royal psalms as unfinished hope, and not as a celebration of political victory already consummated.

politics.title: Babylonian exile as a political and theological crisis
politics.detail: Book Four is described as wrestling with questions raised at the time of the Exile, when it seemed that the alliance with David had been dissolved. Exile is the explicit background of the crisis that shapes the reading of these psalms.
politics.readingImpact: The psalms of this section are read as a liturgical response to a national defeat and the apparent breakdown of the Davidic promises.

politics.title: Post-exile and the final organization of the Psalter
politics.detail: The edition of the book in five collections was completed after Babylonian exile. The note also suggests that the closure of Book Four in Sl 106:48, parallel to 1Cr 16:36, may indicate completion in the post-exile period.
politics.readingImpact: The final form of the book is read as a work of post-exile editors who organized Israel's suffering and hope in a theological sequence.

politics.title: Empire/nation on the horizon of historical psalms
politics.detail: The notes mention that the Psalter preserves memories of the suffering of the Jews in captivity and the expected restoration, especially in psalms like Sl 137, although without detailing the dominant empire beyond Babylonian exile. It is also claimed that the book prepares the people for the submission of the nations to the Messiah.
politics.readingImpact: Conflicts between Israel and foreign powers should be read not only as national events, but as part of the expectation of a universal reign of the Messiah.

customs.title: Liturgical use and Community recitation of psalms
customs.detail: The notes say that the temple stimulated both writing and the collection of psalms, and that many were used in community life. It is also claimed that they were recited and preserved for church/community service.
customs.readingImpact: The psalms should be read as texts of worship, not only as private meditations; their liturgical function helps to explain repetitions, formulas and groupings.

customs.title: Corner with instruments and music accompaniment
customs.detail: The Greek name psalmos and the Hebrew mizmor are connected to the corner accompanied by string instruments. In Sl 150, the notes speak of instruments and dance; flutes are not mentioned as instruments of temple worship, while cymbals were two bronze plates percussed by temple musicians.
customs.readingImpact: This shows that the poetry of the psalms was integrated into real musical practices; the reading must perceive the performative and community character of these texts.

customs.title: Pilgrimage to Jerusalem at the annual festivals
customs.detail: The notes associate Psalms 120-134 with the songs used when the people traveled to Jerusalem for the annual feasts. These ascent songs function as a pilgrimage liturgy.
customs.readingImpact: When reading these psalms, the context is not only individual; they reflect cultual displacement, path and collective worship.

customs.title: Easter and national memory
customs.detail: Tyndale associates Psalms 113-118 with use in the Easter context. Moreover, other psalms recall the historical care of the Lord for Israel, preparing the people to read their own crisis in the light of redemptive memory.
customs.readingImpact: Reading gains a celebrative-historical tone: it is not only devotion, but a ritual memory of God's liberation.

customs.title: Fasting, confession and repentance as practices incorporated into the Psalter
customs.detail: Matthew Henry's introduction points out that the book serves for confession, petition and thanksgiving, and that penance psalms were especially highlighted by Christian devotions. Tyndale's note on additions in Sl 51 and 69 suggests changes of circumstance and new stanzas linked to prayer for restoration of Zion and Jerusalem.
customs.readingImpact: The psalms should not be read as static texts; they reflect practices of repentance, memory and pastoral updating of prayer.

language.title: "Torah" as instruction, not just "law"
language.detail: In Ps 1:2, the note explains that torah is the full revelation of God's instructions. The psalm therefore opens the book as sapiential instruction.
language.readingImpact: Reading ceases to reduce the psalm to legalism; it is a formative teaching for the character and life of the people.

language.title: "Blessing" as the happiness of the righteous
language.detail: The expression "Oh, the joys" in Sl 1:1 is explained as a specific Hebrew term (-ashrey), distinct from blessing in other contexts. The notes contrast the path of the righteous with that of the wicked.
language.readingImpact: The opening of the book emphasizes a happiness linked to the right path before God, not simple external prosperity.

language.title: meditating and night as totalizing practice
language.detail: In Sl 1:2, "Idia and night" is explained as covering all the moments of life; meditating is inner reflection that can be positive or negative, but here it turns to the word of the Lord.
language.readingImpact: The reader understands that the piety of Psalm 1 is continuous and daily, not episodic.

language.title: "Selah" as an uncertain musical/literary term
language.detail: The notes report that Selah appears throughout the book and is probably a musical or literary term, although the exact sense is uncertain. In the NLT it is poured as Interlude.
language.readingImpact: The reader should not overload the term with dogmatic meaning; it marks the poetic and possibly musical progression.

language.title: Structure in five books as an editorial and theological resource
language.detail: The Psalter is organized into five collections with final doxologies in the books 1-4. The division is presented as a result of the editorial work over time, and the salts 1-2 work as an introduction to the entire collection.
language.readingImpact: The form of the book is part of the message: reading must accompany the canonical arrangement, not just isolated psalms.

language.title: Tree, Path and Judgment Images in Sl 1
language.detail: The righteous is compared to the well irrigated tree and the wicked to something carried away by the wind and excluded from judgment. The note explains that the path represents life and character.
language.readingImpact: These images shape the moral reading of the psalm as a contrast between fruitless stability and condemned dispersion.

timeline.title: Composition over about a thousand years
timeline.detail: The introduction states that poets wrote the psalms over a thousand years, while the people recited them and gathered them together in smaller collections that were later incorporated into larger collections.
timeline.readingImpact: This prevents treating the Psalter as the work of a single epoch; it brings together old and later voices under a final edition.

timeline.title: Editorial conclusion after Babylonian exile
timeline.detail: The edition of the Psalter in a single book is described as a process completed after Babylonian exile. Book Four can already reflect this post-exile phase.
timeline.readingImpact: The final form of the book is after several of the individual poems and responds to a community wounded and restored in hope.

timeline.title: Lifetime and post-davics mixed in the corpus
timeline.detail: There are psalms associated with David, Asaph, the descendants of Korah, Solomon, Heman, Ethan, and Moses; in addition, some psalms of David seem to presuppose the temple, which suggests the use of non-strictly authored titles. The notes also observe psalms possibly composed much later, such as Sl 137 at the time of Babylonian captivity.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader must distinguish between the traditional figure of the title and concrete historical composition; the book preserves multiple temporal layers.

timeline.title: Period of exile as a backdrop for Book Four
timeline.detail: Book Four is explicitly linked to the questions arising in the time of Exile, when it seemed that the Davidic alliance had been dissolved.
timeline.readingImpact: The psalms of this section should be read in response to the apparent interruption of the real promises of God.

timeline.title: Jesus" period: the Psalter was already known Scripture
timeline.detail: The notes note that in the time of Jesus the Psalter was well known and integrated the section of the Hebrew canon Writings. Jesus and the apostles quote him widely.
timeline.readingImpact: Christian reading is canonical and retrospective: psalms were already authoritative texts for Jesus and the apostolic church.

timeline.title: Psalm 150 as a programmatic closing of the book
timeline.detail: The last psalm summons everything that breathes to praise the Lord and is presented as a proper conclusion of the whole Psalter.
timeline.readingImpact: The closure guides the reading of the whole book for universal worship and total response to the greatness of God.

investigation: The notes are selective and favor canonical, liturgical and Christological reading; they do not offer complete historical reconstruction of each psalm.
The information about authorship is cautious: the titles may indicate author, dedication, subject or historical relationship, and in several cases the identification remains uncertain.
There is debate about the exact function of titles, musical notes and terms like Selah; the source explicitly recognizes uncertainty.
The internal chronology is broad and approximate: it is spoken in a thousand years, post-exile and Jesus" period, but without exact dates for most psalms.
Some details of worship, such as the precise use of certain psalms in specific ceremonies, are presented as probable or traditional, but the exact nature of community use remains uncertain.
The dossier does not extrapolate into books other than the examples explicitly mentioned in the grades, and does not attempt to harmonize all possible academic proposals.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends only on the annexed notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry, who are introductory and do not intend to solve all historical questions of the Psalter. Therefore, coverage is necessarily selective: there is more material about the structure of the book, traditional authorship, liturgical use and christological reading than about the detailed political context of each psalm. No speculative chronologies or external historical reconstructions were used. Where the source suggests, instead of demonstrating, authorship or date, the answer marks this as interpretation. There are also real gaps in specific customs, economics, social classes and everyday life, because the scores provided deal mainly with worship, poetry and theology. Some technical terms and titles remain uncertain in the sources themselves, and this uncertainty has been preserved rather than being filled in by external knowledge.
